title: Koei Tecmo continues to be an investment firm that also happens to make video games
description: I’ve yet to see Berkshire Hathaway’s psychological horror game. I’ve long been a fan of games by Koei Tecmo, whether it’s their individual classics like Koei’s Dynasty Warriors or Tecmo’s Ninja Gaiden, or modern games like Nioh. content:
I’ve yet to see Berkshire Hathaway’s psychological horror game.

I’ve long been a fan of games by Koei Tecmo, whether it’s their individual classics like Koei’s Dynasty Warriors or Tecmo’s Ninja Gaiden, or modern games like Nioh. They tend not to have major blockbuster releases like some other companies, but it’s a solid lineup of enjoyable titles in an interesting variety of genres.

But there’s another side to Koei Tecmo that you might not be familiar with. To see what that is, let’s take a look at Koei Tecmo Holdings’ recently published Q1 results for the current fiscal year.

コーエーテクモ 2027年3月期1Q ※ゲーム会社です

-------
営業利益：54億700万円

①営業外収益：125億5700万円
-うち 投資有価証券売却益：36億7700万円
-うち 有価証券償還益：18億2100万円
-うち デリバティブ評価益：18億4200万円
-うち 為替差益：4億5500万円

②営業外費用：22億4600万円… pic.twitter.com/6pgPNPUDrQ

— 官報ブログ (@kanpo_blog) July 27, 2026

According to those numbers, Koei Tecmo brought in 5.47 billion yen (US$33 million) in operating income, which is everything related to their game business and not too shabby. However, they eclipsed that with 12.56 billion ($76 million) in non-operational income, which is money earned on things not related to their game business. Taking away non-operational costs, they are left with an ordinary income of 15.72 billion ($96 million) in earnings, only about a third of which is from video games.

That’s an incredible financial safety net that most video game studios would dream of having, and the reason all boils down to one woman: Keiko Erikawa.

▼ “Chairperson Keiko Erikawa is so cool! I’d love a simulation game that lets you manage assets like stocks and real estate.”

襟川恵子会長かっこいい
シュミレーションゲームに株、不動産とかできる資産運用ゲーム出して欲しい https://t.co/tvt4xrovDE pic.twitter.com/xoEdTYNQVM

— ファー (@farfarfarfff) July 29, 2024

Keiko was one of the cofounders of Koei, helping to transition it from a failing dye company to a game studio back in 1978, along with her husband Yoichi. While Yoichi mainly focused on the programming side of things, Keiko was wearing a number of hats, including package art with the help of her background in design at Tama Art University.

While she was in high school, Keiko’s grandmother sparked her interest in stocks. Despite having no formal business education, she taught herself from an early age the importance of risk assessment. This experience was crucial in helping her navigate the ups and downs of the eternally hit-and-miss world of video game creation.

As luck would have it, a number of successes came early on with the historical text-based game The Battle of Kawanakajima and some of the first-ever erotic games, such as Temptation of the Condominium Wife, for microcomputers. This gave way to the breakout success of Nobunaga’s Ambition in 1983, kicking off a series of popular historical strategy games that continues to this day. All this time, Keiko was diligently investing their profits and preparing for a day when their string of successes might dry up.

The irony was that things never really did dry up for Koei. The company just kept chugging along and making profits for decades. Even during the economic bubble burst of Japan in the ’90s and the 2008 financial crisis, Keiko’s well-built financial shield allowed Koei to proceed steadily. Merging with Tecmo and taking on much of their talent and IP in 2009 only made things that much better.

▼ Although a lot can be said about her financial prowess, Keiko Erikawa also pioneered women-oriented games, developing titles such as the Angelique series.

Keiko’s contribution to business and gaming has earned her the nickname “Empress,” which is also extended to both “Empress of the Gaming Industry” and “Empress of Investing.” Comments online continued to bow in reverence to her, while some wondered about Koei Tecmo’s future, as no Empress can rule forever.

“Keiko Erikawa is Japan’s Warren Buffett.”
“She is a living legend.”
“It’s an investment firm. They just make games as a hobby.”
“You have to bow down to such a huge non-operating income.”
“It’s truly amazing how they remain consistently undefeated.”
“The Empress is getting up in years, though. The company might fold without her.”
“She should be in charge of Japan’s funds.”
“They should make an investment simulation game.”

Unlike most companies, Koei Tecmo’s financial management had no advisors, managers, or outside consultants. The buck literally stopped at Keiko Erikawa for nearly all of the company’s history, and as a result, they’ve never once been in debt and never laid off a soul.

Knowing this can’t go on forever, in recent years, she set up a department inside the company where she trains employees to adopt her rules for money management and allow them to continue making video games with a comfortable sense of financial security.

content:
Kabuki adaptation of Studio Ghibli anime masterpiece will be shown online, but you’ll need to mark the date on your calendar.

The live-action kabuki stage play adaptation of Studio Ghibli’s Princes Mononoke is now roughly half-way through its run at Tokyo’s Shinbashi Enbujo Theater. Tickets are almost entirely sold out, so for fans who haven’t already secured theirs, they’re going to be hard to come by.

Thankfully, though, it’s been announced that the Princess Mononoke stage play will be coming to online streaming, but it’s still something that fans will need to clear out a spot on their calendar for.

▼ A preview video for the Princess Mononoke kabuki play, showing Dango Ichikawa as Ashitaka, Kazutaro Nakamura as San, Manju Nakamura as Lady Eboshi, and a number of other human and creature characters from the Ghibli classic.

A live-stream will be shown of the final Princess Mononoke performance, the curtain for which will open at 4 p.m. on August 23. Access to the stream is priced at 4,800 yen (US$30), which is more expensive than the absolute cheapest theater tickets for the performance (3,000 yen), but still quite a bit under the second-lowest-priced seat (6,500 yen).

▼ Another preview video, showing off the kodama forest spirits and some very cool practical effects.

Especially if you’re planning to watch the stream together with a group of friends, it shouldn’t shatter your budget, and if you’re willing to shell out a little more, there’s also a 5,500-yen streaming package that includes a documentary with six months of behind-the-scenes footage chronicling the challenges the cast and crew faced and overcame in bringing one of anime’s most visually distinctive works into the real world.

The stream will be available on Rakuten, Hulu, Kabuki on Demand, and E Plus/Streaming Plus (links below).

title: Tokyo security guard’s famous station tape font becomes official custom Nike streetwear
description: Upgrade your wardrobe with custom clothes featuring the iconic font of a Shinjuku Station legend. When considering what apparel to pick up as a souvenir from your trip to Tokyo, some people might opt for a classic woodblock-style print design, like The Great Wave Off Kanagawa, some may go for a more natural cherry blossom-style […]
content:
Upgrade your wardrobe with custom clothes featuring the iconic font of a Shinjuku Station legend.

When considering what apparel to pick up as a souvenir from your trip to Tokyo, some people might opt for a classic woodblock-style print design, like The Great Wave Off Kanagawa, some may go for a more natural cherry blossom-style design, while others decide on some stylistic Japanese calligraphy. However, now the Nike Shinjuku store has added another possibility into the mix of your future wardrobe, and it’s brought to you by a security guard at Shinjuku Station, famous for his packing-tape typography.

Shuetsu Sato became a Japanese graphic design legend after he started helping the millions of daily commuters navigate Japan’s infamously confusing station construction, cutting bold, rounded directional signs out of cheap, colorful adhesive tape. His handmade font, known as Shuetsu-tai, won over typography enthusiasts worldwide with its warm charm.

Back in 2016, our team interviewed Mr. Shuetsu and asked him to do a live demonstration for our editorial department, where he crafted a beautiful version of our Japanese site’s name right before our eyes.

▼ You can even watch the process of its creation.

Opened on April 10, the Nike Shinjuku store has made his lettering a part of its identity, after an art director hired him for the job, featuring it both on the exterior digital displays and store logo.

However, it doesn’t stop there, as located on the first floor, the Nike By You station lets visitors personalize blank t-shirts and hoodies with exclusive Shuetsu-tai patches.

All you need to do is:

  • Pick your blank t-shirt or hoodie: a small black t-shirt costs 4,620 yen (US$28.20).
  • Choose your patches: a variety of bold Shuetsu-tai letterings, including the iconic Shinjuku logo (“新宿”) or the Just Do It slogan (“ジャストドゥイット”), are on offer, ranging from 550 yen for a small size to 990 yen for a large.

  • Design and press: lay out your patches anywhere you like on the garment and secure them with tape. Once you check out, the store staff heat-presses your design, often being ready in around 20 minutes if not too busy.

Customization is done on a same-day first-come, first-served reservation system and weekend slots for the Nike By You station can fill up fast, but you can usually walk right in on weekday afternoons without a reservation, although it depends on the time slot. The downside is that you won’t be able to know until you visit the store itself, and you’ll also need to sign up for the free Nike Membership through the Nike App.

To show our support for the designer and long-time friend of the site, Mr. Shuetsu, we decided to get the Shinjuku logo right on the front of the shirt, and “Just Do It” on the upper back, which is beautifully modelled here by our fashion icon Mr. Sato.

While we feel the logos might have been better had they been positioned slightly higher, we are pretty satisfied with the final result.

Next time you are thinking of picking up a trendy souvenir you can wear, you should swing by the Nike Shinjuku store to create your own T-shirt or hoodie that has its design roots based on the nearby labyrinthine Shinjuku Station, born from the hand of one of its security guards who just wanted to help more people find their way.

content:
Godiva brings its chocolate expertise to a traditional summertime favorite in Japan.

Godiva is well aware of the worldwide prestige its name carries, but the chocolatier’s Japanese division still frequently looks for ways to get into the spirit of the local sweets scene. Sometimes that means partnerships with anime franchises or Mister Donut, and sometimes it means incorporating traditional Japanese ingredients like tofu into their desserts,

For their next cultural crossover, Godiva Japan is turning its attention to something that’s been a summertime favorite of sweets fans in Japan for generations: shaved ice.

Walking around Japan in the summer, you can spot cafes and sweets shops with signs hanging outside their storefronts with the kanji character for ice, 氷, and as of July 22, they’ll be outside select Godiva Japan branches too. But whereas the majority of shaved ice flavors in Japan are fruity, like melon or strawberry, Godiva, naturally, is bringing its premium chocolate to the mix, starting with the Shaved Ice Chocolat Elegance.

Starting at the bottom of the bowl and working our way up, this extra-chocolatey shaved ice dessert has chocolate whipped cream and shaved chocolate, after which the ice shavings start getting piled on, with chocolate syrup poured on top of them. For toppings, Godiva Japan uses a chocolate whipped cream dusted with chocolate powder, followed by more chocolate sauce and shaved chocolate, then, finally, a Godiva chocolate square as the figurative cherry on top.

If you’re looking for a little extra sophistication, you can also opt for the Shaved Ice Tiramisu Chocolat. This being Godiva, of course there’s still chocolate on the list of ingredients, but here it’s joined by mascarpone cream and coffee gelatin.

According to the company’s announcement, and also visible in the photos, Godiva shaves its ice to a feathery consistency, so there won’t be much crunch or grit as you bite into a spoonful, but instead a soft texture that should allow all of the sweet accouterments to meld in your mouth with the ice. The result, Godiva promises, is richly flavorful but without feeling heavy, and the moist, chilled combination of flavors and sensations will make for an indulgently enjoyable way to cool off in the summer heat.

Not every Godiva Japan branch will be serving their shaved ice, but it can be found at the chain’s locations within the Mitsui Outlet Park shopping centers in Tama Minami Osawa (Tokyo), Kisarazu (Chiba), Iruma (Saitama), Hokuriku Oyabe (Toyama), Jazz Dream Nagashima (Mie), Shiga Ryuo (Shiga), Marine Pia Kobe (Hyogo), and Spporo Kitahiroshima (Hokkaido).

Godiva Japan’s new frozen treats arrive at a time when a number of cafes in Japan are looking to take shaved ice up-market with fancy ingredients, but priced at 980 yen (US$6) they’re still affordable luxuries for when your taste buds want something sweet and your body needs something cool this summer.

title: Tokyo’s newest viral dessert is like a Japanese parfait inside a bread bun [Taste test]
description: A cool idea from Coolish, and further proof that sweet bean paste makes everything better. When you’re craving a snack, anpan (sweet bean paste bread) is never, ever a bad choice. Both sweet and substantial, anpan can be found at convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, but if you want the really good stuff, it’s […]
content:
A cool idea from Coolish, and further proof that sweet bean paste makes everything better.

When you’re craving a snack, anpan (sweet bean paste bread) is never, ever a bad choice. Both sweet and substantial, anpan can be found at convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, but if you want the really good stuff, it’s worth it to seek this treat out at dedicated bakeries, which is what recently had us on the train to Mitaka Station in Tokyo.

We were headed there to visit Toho Bakery, because while they’re not the only bakery in town that has anpan, they’re the only ones that have ice cream anpan.

Toho Bakery is a 10-minute bus ride from Mitaka Station, or a 25-minute walk if you’re feeling energetic/want to pre-bank some calories to spare before you enjoy this tempting double dessert. Whether you arrive by bus or on foot, though, it’s pretty easy to tell you’re in the right place, thanks to the bakery’s large-font signage and giant illustrated baker with an oversized baguette.

The ice cream anpan is a Toho project carried out in official conjunction with Japanese confectioner Lotte, maker of ice cream brand Coolish, which is so tasty that it can even bring virtual idols into the real world. Coolish’s hook is that it’s a drinkable soft ice cream sold in squeeze pouches…but what if instead of squeezing the ice cream into your mouth, you squeezed it into a piece of anpan?

That’s the idea Toho Bakery and Lotte came up with, and so in late June Toho started whipping up batches of Coolish-use Anpan.

If you’re wondering why they didn’t just call it “Coolish Anpan,” it’s because the baking process required to create bread is equally effective at melting ice cream, and so the Coolish has to be injected into the baked goods after they come out of the oven. What’s more, as a classy place that prides itself on high quality, Toho Bakery doesn’t want to pre-inject the ice cream before purchase and then leave the anpan to get soggy on the store’s shelves, so the 356-yen (US$2.20) Coolish-use Anpan is a set of one anpan bun and a mini Coolish pouch that’s given to you at the register, after which you squeeze in the ice cream yourself.

However, don’t make the mistake of assuming the Coolish-use Anpan is just a marketing name for a bundle of regular anpan and a Coolish. Toho Bakery actually created a different type of anpan specifically for this set. The sweet bean paste filling is less sweet than the bakery’s normal anpan, since it’s going to get an extra infusion of sweetness when the ice cream comes flowing in. The bread is also sized/shaped so that it has an air pocket at the top, giving it space for the ice cream to settle inside.

▼ Proportionally, the Coolish-use Anpan is taller than normal anpan, which usually has more of a dome shape.

Ice cream being a key ingredient means that time is a factor with the Coolish-use Anpan, and if you’ve got a long train ride home from Toho Bakery, taking an insulated bag and some ice packs with you wouldn’t be a bad idea. Of course, there are few things in life more difficult than resisting the urge to eat ice cream when you have some in your possession, and thankfully Toho Bakery has a few outdoor seats and tables where you can enjoy your bread immediately after buying it, which is what we did.

Coolish pouches have a pronounced plastic mouth, and while the original intended purpose is to make the pouch easier to drink from, this design point also makes it easy to stab the mouth through the top layer of the bun. Because the Coolish had just been taken out of the freezer, it was harder than usual, so it took a couple of strong squeezes to get it all in there…

…but we persevered.

Now it was time to taste the completed Coolish-use Anpan, and on a hot summer afternoon, it was pretty much perfect! Ice cream and sweet bean paste come from very different culinary lineages, but they actually go together extremely well, especially since Toho Bakery uses tsubuan, the type of sweet bean paste in which some beans are left unmashed, adding some enticing texture to the creamy mix that results from the addition of the Coolish. With a mixture of sweet and creamy flavors, the Coolish-use Anpan ends up being like a Japanese-style parfait that you can hold in your hand.

Now, if you’re thinking “Hey, couldn’t I squirt some Coolish into the anpan they sell at the convenience store closest to my apartment/hotel/ninja testing center in Japan?” the answer is yes, you can, and we can’t imagine it’d be anything short of delicious too. Like we said above, though, Toho Bakery’s Coolish-use Anpan is designed to make the combination as harmonious as possible, in terms of both flavor balancing and physical space.

▼ Some of Lotte’s official Coolish-use Anpan press photos

So if you can make it to Toho Bakery, it’s worth the trip to try the ultimate version of this sweets innovation, which is scheduled to be on sale until August 8, or while supplies last.

title: Starbucks Japan opens new store inside historic seaside quarantine station near Tokyo
description: Sip on Starbucks in a setting once linked to infectious diseases. Whenever a historic building in a prime location in Japan needs a commercial tenant, there’s a good chance Starbucks will come knocking. With a solid track record of taking up residence in some of the country’s most unique and culturally important properties, the coffee […]
content:
Sip on Starbucks in a setting once linked to infectious diseases.

Whenever a historic building in a prime location in Japan needs a commercial tenant, there’s a good chance Starbucks will come knocking. With a solid track record of taking up residence in some of the country’s most unique and culturally important properties, the coffee chain has shown it knows how to adapt its brand to blend seamlessly into its surroundings, respecting historic features while enhancing the original character of a building.

So when the Yokohama city government sought applicants to occupy the former No. 1 Building of the Nagahama Quarantine Station, a Registered Tangible Cultural Property, it wasn’t too much of a surprise to hear that Starbucks was chosen to be its new custodian. What was a surprise, though, was the history of the charming, Western-style building, which dates back to 1895, when it was originally built as a waiting facility for passengers undergoing quarantine inspections after arriving by ship.

During this era, the port city of Yokohama was Japan’s main international entry point, and the quarantine station played an important role in preventing infectious diseases from entering the country via overseas ships. Though the building was damaged in the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923, it was restored the following year, and recently relocated to a site within Umi no Koen (Sea Park), after extensive preservation work.

▼ Umi no Koen is roughly an hour by train from Tokyo.


Now the historic building is opening the door to a new chapter, with one half becoming a Starbucks cafe, and the other half being used as an exhibition space run by Yokohama City and Umi no Koen’s management. Through historical displays and community events, the exhibition wing aims to preserve and share the story of the former quarantine station with visitors.

▼ Left: Starbucks Bar Counter (バーカウンター) and Cafe (カフェ); Right: Exhibition Room (展示室), Rest Area (休憩室), and entrance (入口).

Rather than modernising the interior, Starbucks says it has retained many of the building’s original features. Original wallpaper from the Taishō era (1912–1926) has been preserved where possible, while bentwood chairs and other carefully selected furnishings complement the architecture, creating a space that feels more like a heritage lounge than a typical coffee shop.

▼ The planned interior for the cafe.

From its location inside Umi no Koen, the store boasts a scenic waterfront setting that’s especially popular during summer, making it an appealing stop for visitors looking to combine sightseeing, seaside strolls and a coffee break away from central Tokyo.

This location is the latest in a growing list of new openings for Starbucks, which includes the recently opened Yanaka branch in Tokyo, the teahouse in Kyoto’s oldest public park, and even the branch on a Shinkansen platform in Yokohama. We can’t wait to see how Starbucks blends its modern stylings into the historic character of this building when it opens to the public on 10 August.

title: Japan’s foreign resident population hits record high as Japanese population hits record low
description: The number of Japanese citizens falls below 120 million for the first time in 42 years, but the foreign community continues to grow. Japan’s population has been shifting more than ever in recent years, with declining births becoming a growing concern for the country. However, new data shows that the population decline is being partially […]
content:
The number of Japanese citizens falls below 120 million for the first time in 42 years, but the foreign community continues to grow.

Japan’s population has been shifting more than ever in recent years, with declining births becoming a growing concern for the country. However, new data shows that the population decline is being partially offset by a growing number of foreign residents, who are taking up residence in Japan in greater numbers than ever before.

According to population data released by Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications on 29 July, the number of Japanese citizens stood at 119,736,483 as of 1 January 2026, dropping below 120 million for the first time since 1984.

The figure represents a decrease of around 917,000 people compared with the previous year, marking the largest annual decline since the survey began in 1968.

The decline reflects Japan’s ongoing demographic challenges, with the country’s ageing population and falling birth rate continuing to accelerate population loss. Japan recorded around 1.59 million deaths, while the number of births fell to a record low of approximately 670,000.

▼ The number of Japanese citizens has now fallen for 17 consecutive years.

Looking at the figures by prefecture, 46 of Japan’s 47 prefectures saw their Japanese populations decline. Tokyo was the only exception, with numbers rising by 0.09 percent. The largest decrease was recorded in Akita Prefecture, which fell by 1.95 percent, followed by Aomori and Kochi, both of which declined by 1.70 percent.

As the number of Japanese citizens continues to decrease, the foreign resident population continues to grow. The number of foreign residents increased by around 354,000 people year-on-year to reach 4,031,159, the highest figure since the survey began tracking this data in 2013.

▼ Unlike the Japanese population, the foreign resident population increased in every prefecture across Japan, not just in Tokyo.

The contrasting trends highlight Japan’s shifting demographics, as a shrinking domestic population is increasingly being offset by a growing number of people from overseas living in the country. With Japan’s massive tourism boom leading to record numbers of overseas visitors in 2025, the foreign population looks likely to grow even further, even as the government moves to implement stricter new requirements for permanent resident applicants.

content:
Cleverly designed jewellery sways while you wear it, just like Kasuga-sama does in the animated film.

Japan is a country filled with stories of mysterious spirits, characters and costumes, and some of them appear in Studio Ghibli’s 2001 anime film, Spirited Away.

One such character is Kasuga-sama, a spirit that crosses the bridge to the bathhouse wearing a distinctive white mask with eerie face-like marks. Despite only spending a short time on screen, its striking appearance makes it one of the most memorable characters in the film.

While some might think the mask is an original idea born from the creative mind of director Hayao Miyazaki, it bears a striking resemblance to the traditional zomen paper mask used in a Bugaku dance at Nara’s Kasuga Taisha shrine. Even Kasuga Taisha once commented on the resemblance by sharing a photo with the message: “This is a zomen mask used in the Bugaku dance Soriko. (…It’s Kasuga-sama.)”

【お面】
雑面
蘇利古という曲で使われるお面です。

(…春日様だ)#春日大社#奈良 #舞楽#南都楽所#縦長サムネ pic.twitter.com/I41nIeg394

— 春日大社 kasugataisha shrine (@KASUGASHRINE) May 26, 2021

Bugaku is a type of ancient Japanese court dance performed to the accompaniment of Gagaku, Japan’s classical imperial court music. With a history stretching back more than 1,200 years, it remains one of Japan’s oldest performing arts, and Soriko is one of the traditional dances still preserved today.

The anime character, who shares the same name as the shrine, becomes even more fascinating after learning about its connections to Japanese culture, and now we can keep that history close to our minds with a new product from Ghibli specialty retail chain Donguri Kyowakoku.

Called the “Kasuga-sama Spirited Away Tassel Earrings”, these beautiful fashion accessories bring the character to life, with the eye-catching mask sitting on the ear lobe…

▼ … and the red “cloak” swaying behind the ear as a bright red tassel.

The earrings are part of a new line of accessories called “Mori no Pomponne”, which features motifs and characters from Ghibli movies. The brand name appears to combine the Japanese word mori (“forest”) with the French word pomponner, meaning “to dress up” or “to get dressed up”, reflecting the collection’s focus on wearable accessories that combine elegance with a touch of playfulness.

▼ This design reflects that ethos, with the red tassel swaying gently to replicate the movement of the character from the film.

The earrings are around five centimetres (two inches) long, made from zinc alloy, polyester, iron, surgical stainless steel and epoxy resin, and weigh three grams (0.1 ounces) per earring.

Available in both pierced and clip-on versions, the earrings are priced at 3,630 yen (US$25) per pair and can be purchased from 10 a.m. on 1 August at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (pierced version here and clip-ons here), while stocks last.

title: 7-Eleven Japan adds new cold soup smoothies to its convenience store drinks range
description: Cold soup smoothies are good for the gut and good for the ‘Gram. Ever since 7-Eleven completed its rollout of smoothie machines at around 18,000 stores in Japan in 2024, the chain has been experimenting with all sorts of unique ingredients, giving us everything from coffee through to matcha and even sweet potato varieties. Now, […]
content:
Cold soup smoothies are good for the gut and good for the ‘Gram.

Ever since 7-Eleven completed its rollout of smoothie machines at around 18,000 stores in Japan in 2024, the chain has been experimenting with all sorts of unique ingredients, giving us everything from coffee through to matcha and even sweet potato varieties.

Now, the chain is rethinking the whole concept of smoothies, by announcing the release of two new “Cold Soup Smoothies” that blur the line between sweet drink and nourishing meal with an interesting blend of ingredients.

▼ The first new variety is the Fruit Gazpacho Smoothie.

Like all of the chain’s smoothies, these new varieties are sold frozen, with chopped ingredients inside that are whipped up by dedicated machines operated by customers at the counter. The gazpacho variety is inspired by the classic chilled Spanish soup, and features a blend of cherry tomatoes, paprika, and watermelon juice blended with whole lemons, including the peel, for a refreshing summer drink that contains both sweet and savoury notes.

▼ The juice component is cleverly frozen into cubes, matching the size of the other ingredients to create a well-balanced blend of texture and flavour.

▼ Then we have the Grilled Corn Smoothie.

Designed to recreate the flavour of freshly grilled corn, this drink combines roasted sweetcorn with oligosaccharides and fermented rice bran, creating a creamy cold soup with a smoky sweetness.

▼ Oligosaccharides are a type of prebiotic carbohydrate that helps to nourish beneficial gut bacteria.

As the somewhat fancier-than-normal ingredients suggest, these drinks aren’t your typical, run-of-the-mill convenience store product. That’s because rather than developing the drinks entirely in-house, 7-Eleven brought together experts from several fields to create the recipes.

Chef Tatsuya Noda from Innovative Kitchen 8go, a restaurant known for its “regenerative” approach to cooking and reducing food waste, worked on developing the well-rounded flavour…

▼ … while Bacterico, a company specialising in gut microbiome research, contributed nutritional expertise.

The collaboration was coordinated through GIC Tokyo (Gastronomy Innovation Campus Tokyo), a food innovation hub operated by Tokyo Tatemono that brings chefs, researchers and businesses together to develop new food concepts.

By incorporating “regenerative” food production into the new release, 7-Eleven is able to save food and edible byproducts that might otherwise go to waste. The Grilled Corn Smoothie, for example, contains fermented rice bran developed by Fermenstation, which makes us of a rice milling byproduct while adding nutritional benefits for gut health.

According to 7-Eleven, customers are increasingly viewing smoothies as not only a tasty drink but a healthy meal option, so creating a new soup-style variety is said to be a natural next step in catering to these needs.

▼ 冷製スープ = Chilled Soup

Though hot canned soup in vending machines has long been a thing in Japan, we’ve never seen cold soup smoothies before, and with professional chefs and gut health specialists overseeing the process, these look set to become the next big viral convenience store trend to flood your socials.

The new smoothies are only being sold in limited areas of Tokyo, though, with the Fruit Gazpacho Smoothie available at select stores in Chuo Ward while the Grilled Corn Smoothie will be available at select stores in Chuo and Chiyoda wards.

Released on 28 July, each variety is priced at 462 yen (US$3.10) plus tax, and will be sold in the standing freezer section for customers to whip up fresh at smoothie machines on the counter after purchasing them.

title: New service lets Tokyo tourists display their faces on giant screen at Japan’s busiest intersection
description: Pedestrian crossing outside Shibuya Station to lean even harder into tourist selfie appeal. Shibuya’s Scramble Crossing is one of Tokyo’s most iconic locations, and some would say that a trip to Japan’s capital isn’t complete without stopping by to snap a photo. Soon, though, tourists won’t just be taking photos at the world-famous intersection outside […]
content:
Pedestrian crossing outside Shibuya Station to lean even harder into tourist selfie appeal.

Shibuya’s Scramble Crossing is one of Tokyo’s most iconic locations, and some would say that a trip to Japan’s capital isn’t complete without stopping by to snap a photo. Soon, though, tourists won’t just be taking photos at the world-famous intersection outside Shibuya Station, but displaying them too, on one of Tokyo’s largest skyscraper-side video screens.

Tentatively titled Shibuya Scramble Crossing Photo, this service will allow individuals to have their photos displayed on Q’s Eye, the video screen mounted on the side of Q Front, a building across the Scramble Crossing that houses a Starbucks (and was one of the last places in Tokyo where you could rent VHS tapes). Shibuya Scramble Crossing Photo actually had a brief test run between July 24 and 26, during which 48 people had their pictures put up on the screen for 15 seconds each, with their faces appearing inside a cute illustration evoking Shibuya’s famously loyal dog/statue Hachiko.

渋谷スクランブル交差点の大型ビジョンに、自分の顔が映る!? 東急が新たなインバウンド向けの観光体験サービスを実証実験。デザインや演出など、参加した外国人観光客にもお話を聞きました。世界的観光スポット・渋谷は、次のステージへ。https://t.co/JyZ735Y3dm

— 渋谷文化 (@shibuya_bunka) July 30, 2026

Though the service, offered through rail company and property developer Tokyu, won’t be exclusively available to foreign tourists, they’re the primary intended market, with all of the test-run participants being travelers from Germany, India, Italy, Korea, the U.S.A., Vietnam, or elsewhere overseas. Selfie-snapping is a priority for the service, with Tokyo taking participant feedback into account to try to determine the optimum times to offer displays at, since the screen itself doesn’t photograph as nicely during midday, but the tourists themselves can be obscured in shadow when photographed at night. One participant said he would like to be able to select alternate frames/artwork or add some sort of background music when his photo is displayed, and Tokyu itself says it’s looking for ways to let participants add personalized on-screen text messages or purchase merchandise showing their photo as it appeared on Q’s Eye. Tokyu also wants to shorten the lead time from the current six days down and eventually allow travelers to have their picture up on the screen for everyone to see on the same day they apply for the service.

On the one hand, Shibuya Scramble Crossing Photo makes for a uniquely personalized photo opportunity, and is sure to appeal to travelers who think half the fun of going somewhere is posting photos online showing that you were there. On the other hand, this could nudge the crossing’s environment even farther towards being a total circus, further frustrating locals who are growing increasingly tired of having to dodge tourists who stop mid-intersection and turn their back to the flow of foot traffic as they pose for their selfies.

Tokyu does seem to have crowd control concerns in mind, as one reason for the test run was to assess safety issues. Participants were told in advance when their photos would be displayed, and the Q Front screen is visible/photographable from the Hachiko statue plaza on the station side of the intersection, so there’s no need to stand in the middle of the crossing in order to get a selfie with your on-screen photo in the background. However, this then runs the risk of adding to the congestion of the already crowded plaza if multiple photos are going to be displayed on Q’s Eye in rapid succession.

Prices for Shibuya Scramble Crossing Photo are expected to be in the range of 5,000 to 10,000 yen (approximately US$30-US$60), with the service slated to officially start in March of next year.

content:
Ghibli designs so charming they’ll be hard to peel yourself away from.

Studio Ghibli fans are spoilt for choice when it comes to ways to add a dash of movie magic into their everyday lives, and now there’s a range that’ll stick with you both figuratively and literally.

This latest release is a new addition to the washi tape range from Ghibli’s GBL brand, which prides itself on its cool “American casual” style aesthetic. Though they’re recoginsable to Japanese stationery fans as “washi tape”, so-called as they’re made with Japanese washi paper, GBL adheres to its American style influences by referring to them as “masking tape” instead.

Whatever you choose to call them, these sticky tapes can be used to help seal up wrapped packages, decorate journals and calendars, or stick photos, postcards and notes in place without leaving any sticky residue behind.

▼ Each tape features memorable scenes and motifs from various Ghibli films.

▼ The latest releases adds three new designs to the range, with two dedicated to Porco Rosso and one to My Neighbour Totoro.

▼ Porco Rosso: Piccolo S.P.A.

This cool design features the logo of Piccolo S.P.A., the long-established seaplane manufacturer where star character Porco takes his beloved aircraft for repairs. It’s a subtle choice that captures the look of a vintage aviation brand while looking stylishly modern at the same time.

▼ Porco Rosso: Air Pirate Alliance

Featuring the colourful “flying boats” of the air pirate gangs from Porco Rosso, this lively design has the Dabohaze aircraft leading the formation, with Curtis coming up the rear.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro: Hide-and-Seek

Star character Mei, in her distinctive straw hat, races through colourful leaves as she chases after the Little Totoro and Medium Totoro in this playful woodland design, perfectly capturing one of the film’s most heartwarming moments.

Each roll measures 1.8 centimetres (0.7 inches) wide and 7 metres (276 inches) long, making them ideal for all sorts of sticky situations. All three tapes can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) for 495 yen (US$3.35) each while stocks last.

content:
7-Eleven will finally let you buy baked-in-store pizza without making you buy a whole pizza.

When 7-Eleven Japan announced that they were going to start selling cooked-in-store pizza, it felt like both a no-brainer and a head-scratcher. Let’s start with the first half of that. 7-Eleven Japan has a reputation for excellent food quality, and through their Seven Cafe Bakery System, they already offer a variety of items that are baked in the store, such as melon bread, curry bread, croissants, and cookies. So since they’ve already got the equipment necessary for baking, why not bake pizzas too?

Now we come to the head-scratcher part, though, which was that if you wanted some 7-Eleven pizza, they made you buy a whole pizza. Granted, it wasn’t a particularly huge pizza, but still, you had to purchase the entire thing.

▼ 7-Eleven Japan pizzas, one of which provided us with the materials for a very tasty taste test.

But isn’t one of the major appeals of a convenience store the ability to pop in and pick up a perfectly sized snack for yourself? Pizza cravings don’t always wait until we’re hungry enough to eat a whole pie, and when they do hit, we’re often not strong enough to resist them until we can put together a team to share a whole pizza with either. When your stomach is saying “I want a slice of pizza,” your heart knows that it’s a request that should be granted with all haste, and so we’re happy to report that 7-Eleven Japan is now, finally, selling baked-in-store pizza by the slice.

As of July 28, 7-Eleven Japan is offering two different types of pizza by the slice, occupying what you could say are two opposite ends on the spectrum of traditionalism. Pictured above is their Margherita, a classical creating what 7-Eleven calls “an exquisite balance” between the flavors of its mozzarella cheese, tomato, and basil.

On the other hand, those craving a more localized and contemporarily creative combination of toppings can opt for the teriyaki chicken pizza, which in addition to Japan cuisine’s representative sauce also has rich mayo. 7-Eleven’s preview photo also pretty clearly shows kernels of corn, which aren’t mentioned in the company’s official announcement, but this is Japan, after all, where it’s pretty much always a good idea to be prepared for possible corn on your pizza.

The Margherita is priced at 270 yen (US$1.65) per slice, while the teriyaki chicken is just a touch more, at 290 yen.

Pizza by the slice is being introduced gradually at individual branches, but has begun showing up in 7-Eleven stores in the Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokuriku regions of Japan, along with Hokkaido and Niigata Prefectures, as of July 28. It’ll be coming to the Tokai, Kinki, Chugoku, Shikoku, and Kyushu areas, plus Yamanashi, Nagano, and Okinawa Prefectures, starting August 11.

title: Okayama man arrested for catching butterflies in central Japan
description: It’s becoming a regular Gotham City out there. Things just aren’t the way they used to be in Japan. It wasn’t too long ago that it used to be safe for a butterfly to flutter by down the street without worrying about being kidnapped and killed. Now, with all these kids getting corrupted by the […]
content:
It’s becoming a regular Gotham City out there.

Things just aren’t the way they used to be in Japan. It wasn’t too long ago that it used to be safe for a butterfly to flutter by down the street without worrying about being kidnapped and killed. Now, with all these kids getting corrupted by the likes of National Geographic, Jean-Henri Fabre, and possibly rap music, insects have to constantly live in fear of being skewered and put on display by some insecticidal collector.

Luckily, police are stepping in to protect our six-legged friends, starting with the arrest of a 55-year-old man in Okayama for catching butterflies. These weren’t just any old butterflies, however; they were the rare Kohyomon Modoki (Mellicta ambigua niphona), found in northeast China, South Korea, and in some parts of central Japan.

▼ The best way to capture a Kohyomon Modoki is on video.

Their numbers have been steadily decreasing due to loss of habitat and they were put on the endangered list in 2023. One of the few remaining places to find them is Norikura Kogen, a resort located near the Kita Alps in Nagano Prefecture. It would seem the locals there are very protective of their butterflies because the Ministry of the Environment quickly began receiving reports of someone attempting to capture their Kohyomon Modoki.

Local police were put on alert and on 21 July spotted a suspicious person carrying an insect net. He was promptly arrested on suspicion of violating the Act on Conservation of Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. The suspect admitted to the charges, saying: “I knew I wasn’t supposed to catch them, but I wanted to because they’re rare butterflies.”

Online comments felt that the fact he knew about the butterflies’ situation made his crime more serious. On the other hand, others questioned whether people like him are the real threat to wildlife that we should be worried about.

“It’s one thing if a child caught it by accident, but this person knew what he was doing.”
“These creatures spend years underground and beat the odds by avoiding predators, only to get caught by a human before they can reproduce.”
“He was trying to catch and got caught himself.”
“I saw an old guy swinging a net around Mt. Ontake, too.”
“That person clearly knew what they were doing.”
“The decline of this butterfly is due to the environment. The population won’t shrink just because a few people catch them in nets. If we want them to survive, we need to protect their habitat.”
“Funny how catching a single specimen makes the news but the widespread destruction of their environment that made them endangered in the first place doesn’t.”

The suspect in this case faces punishment in the form of up to five years in prison or a maximum fine of five million yen (US$30,000). More severe penalties are likely reserved for those intending to traffic and profit from the capture of endangered species, but given this man’s clear knowledge of the butterfly’s rarity, that’s not out of the question either and is currently pending investigation.

However, some of those comments made an astute point that we often go after and punish those who interfere with endangered species, but rarely do you ever hear of anyone being held accountable for a species becoming endangered in the first place.

content:
New Japan-exclusive collectibles are only available at select locations.

Japan is famous for gacha capsule toys, and now Starbucks is finally joining the fun with its very first collection of gacha-style collectibles.

Released as part of the chain’s 30th anniversary celebrations in Japan, the new “Starbucks Joyful Capsule” collection consists of nine different plush charms inspired by some of the chain’s most iconic beverages and food items.

Each palm-sized charm comes sealed inside a capsule measuring approximately 7.5 centimetres (3 inches) in diameter, with the design remaining a surprise until it’s opened. Every plush comes with a hook attachment so you can easily clip them onto bags and pouches or even connect multiple charms together.

Some stores will dispense the capsules through traditional gacha machines, while others will sell them over the counter, although Starbucks notes that sales methods may change depending on the store. Each capsule in the five-piece standard collection costs 880 yen (US$5.40).

▼ Double Tall Latte (To Go)

▼ Caramel Macchiato (For Here)

▼ Tokyo Roast

▼ Matcha Cream Frappuccino

▼ Sugar Doughnut

Customers at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo will also be able to pick up an exclusive second collection called Starbucks Reserve Joyful Capsule, featuring four designs inspired by signature drinks and food sold at the Roastery. These capsules are slightly more expensive, at 1,100 yen each.

▼ Caffe Americano (To Go)

▼ Caffe Latte (For Here)

▼ Tokyo Roastery Microblend

▼ Cornetti Crema

While the Roastery collection will be exclusively sold at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo, the standard range will be available at the following 19 Starbucks stores in Tokyo.

  • Shinjuku Southern Terrace*
  • Shibuya Modi

* These stores will sell the capsules via capsule toy machines.

The charms all measure approximately 5-8 centimetres, depending on the design, and are said to be suitable for ages 15 and up. Starbucks will initially be limiting sales to two per transaction, in an effort to ensure as many customers as possible have a chance to purchase them, as these look set to become a sell-out hit.

Though the chain announced that both ranges would be available from 2 August, it has now said that in light of the 28 July earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture, which resulted in a number of fatalities, it has decided to postpone the release. Starbucks says it will notify the public of the new release date as soon as it’s decided, and we will update this page with the new date when it’s announced.

title: Kumamoto Castle left illuminated all night long as symbol of hope for earthquake victims
description: The castle itself is still undergoing repairs from an earthquake from 10 years ago. Kumamoto is still reeling from a massive earthquake that struck the prefecture on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu on the afternoon of July 28. Recovering from the magnitude-7.1 quake will not be a quick or easy process, and there are many, […]
content:
The castle itself is still undergoing repairs from an earthquake from 10 years ago.

Kumamoto is still reeling from a massive earthquake that struck the prefecture on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu on the afternoon of July 28. Recovering from the magnitude-7.1 quake will not be a quick or easy process, and there are many, many difficult days ahead. In dark times, though, any symbol of hope becomes vital, and Kazufumi Onishi, mayor of Kumamoto Prefecture’s Capital of Kumamoto City, shared one the day following the disaster.

今夜は熊本城を夜通しライトアップします
苦しい状況が続きますが、熊本のシンボル・天守閣を見上げて、また明日へ向かって頑張りましょう。 pic.twitter.com/yHYwBRu9Xf

— 熊本市長 大西一史 (@K_Onishi) July 29, 2026

“Tonight, Kumamoto Castle will be illuminated throughout the night,” Onishi announced via his official Twitter account. “We are still dealing with a harsh, difficult situation, but let’s look towards the castle’s tower, the symbol of Kumamoto, and then turn towards doing our best again tomorrow to get through this.”

Kumamoto Castle itself was severely damaged 10 years ago when a previous earthquake struck the region. It took five years for the main keep to be repaired to a state where it could again start welcoming visitors, and restoration work is still ongoing for some parts of the castle. All of that, though, arguably makes it an even more appropriate symbol of resilience, and the decision to keep the castle lit up as a beacon of hope was met with high praise from commenters to Onishi’s announcement.

“In times like this, people really do need a symbol to rally around.”
“The beautiful light of hope.”
“This is a reminder that aside from just food, clothing, and shelter, things like this can have a huge positive effect by providing psychological support. I believe that seeing the castle shining against the night sky will give people the strength to get through this and keep moving forward.”
“Things will get better! Hang in there!”
“I hope the glow of Kumamoto Castle will provide even a little comfort to everyone who’s suffering.”
“No matter how bad things may seem, having something like this that lights up the town is a source of emotional strength. One step at a time, let’s keep doing what we can.”

Usually, on nights when Kumamoto Castle is illuminated, the lights go off sometime between 10 p.m. and midnight. It’s unclear whether the all-night light-up was a one-time only event or whether it’ll be happening periodically as Kumamoto continues to pick up the pieces. Either way, though, it’s nice for people to have a shared symbol of the community to remind them that they’re not alone in these trying times.

title: Katana of one of Japan’s most famous swordsmen goes on display to help Kumamoto earthquake victims
description: The sword of the vice-captain of the Shinsengumi is being called into action once again in a touching story of repaying kindness. On Tuesday morning, a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture, on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu. While the full extent of the damage is still being assessed, at least 30 people are known to […]
content:
The sword of the vice-captain of the Shinsengumi is being called into action once again in a touching story of repaying kindness.

On Tuesday morning, a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture, on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu. While the full extent of the damage is still being assessed, at least 30 people are known to have lost their lives, with hundreds injured, thousands forced to evacuate, and tens of thousands dealing with power outages and water supply disruptions.

In the wake of the disaster, many are looking for ways to help the victims, and one surprising source of aid is going to be Hijikata Toshizo.

Born in 1835, Toshizo (pictured at the top of this article) was a member of the Shinsengumi, a group of swordsmen loyal to the Shogunate who operated in Kyoto during the final years of the Edo period. As the unit’s vice-commander, Toshizo features prominently in both the actual history of the Shinsengumi as well as its many romanticized retellings in film, anime, and video games, and his folk hero status draws admirers and history buffs to the Hijikata Toshizo Museum in Tokyo’s Hino district, where he was born.

The museum is a treasure trove of historical artifacts related to Toshizo’s life and times, but it does not have a large staff. Instead, the museum is managed directly by Toshizo’s descendants, and the modest scale of operations means that it’s only open for a few days every month. On Wednesday, though, the museum announced that it has decided to open on the previously unscheduled August 1 and 2. The museum will be displaying Toshizo’s prized katana, the Izumi no Kami Kanesada, on both days, with all admission fees to be donated to relief efforts for victims of the Kumamoto quake.

▼ The Izumi no Kami Kanesada

熊本県で発生した地震で被災された皆様に心よりお見舞い申し上げます

土方歳三資料館は、8月1日(土)・2日(日)12〜16時に臨時開館し、土方歳三愛刀・和泉守兼定を特別公開いたします。
両日いただいた入館料は、熊本県の文化財保全への寄附に充てさせていただきます。皆様のご協力をお願いいたします… pic.twitter.com/FWmg74imtE

— 土方歳三資料館 (@toshizoofficial) July 29, 2026

This isn’t just a way for the museum to offer support to Kumamoto, but a way for the museum to give something back to the prefecture’s people. The Hijikata Toshizo Museum first opened in 1994, but in 2022 it made the decision shut down for an extended period, as other pressing responsibilities were making it difficult for the family to continue running it. The museum wouldn’t reopen until 2024, but in the meantime, a significant portion of its collection was taken into the care of the Kumamoto Prefectural Museum of Art, who cared for the artifacts and displayed them in special exhibitions, continuing the Hijikata Toshizo Museum’s mission of sharing this part of Japanese history with visitors.

So now the Hijikata Toshizo Museum feels that it’s its turn to lend a hand, saying:

“During the period from 2022 to 2024 in which our museum was closed, the Kumamoto Prefectural Museum of Art kindly hosted [a special Hijikata Toshizo exhibition], and our gratitude to the people of Kumamoto is beyond what we can express in words. We are only a small, individually run museum, but even in some small way, we hope, along with our visitors, to help preserve the culture of Kumamoto into the future.”

The Hijikata Toshizo Museum is just a two-minute walk from Manganji Station on the Tama Toshi Monorail Line, and will be open from noon to 4 p.m. on August 1 and 2, with admission costing 800 yen (US$4.90).

Update: The museum has announced that due to expected ticket demand on August 1 and 2, admission will be by online reservation, with reservations opening through the website here at 9 p.m. on July 30.

title: Sanrio’s newest item looks like dog butt, exactly like it’s supposed to [Photos]
description: If you’ve ever wanted to take a nap while burying your face in Pompompurin’s butthole, this is the cushion you’ve been waiting for. You can make a strong argument that no other company on the planet understands the value of good visual design as well as Sanrio does. Hello Kitty and her friends largely flipped […]
content:
If you’ve ever wanted to take a nap while burying your face in Pompompurin’s butthole, this is the cushion you’ve been waiting for.

You can make a strong argument that no other company on the planet understands the value of good visual design as well as Sanrio does. Hello Kitty and her friends largely flipped the script on character merchandising, in that instead of starting with extensive narratives in animation, books, or other media, Sanrio characters tend to debut as merchandise and build their initial, fundamental fanbases based on their visual atmosphere, with the characters who prove to be the most popular then going on to have their personalities and storylines fleshed out in Netflix series, crossovers with violent sci-fi war epics, and the like.

So it might be surprising, maybe even disappointing, to learn that the appearance of the latest creation from Sanrio’s designers can be described as “total dog but,” or even “complete canine anus,” if you’re in the mood for alliteration and ass-related assonance. However, this isn’t a swing and a miss by Sanrio’s designers, as all of that is by design, because this isn’t just any dog butt we’re talking about here, but Pompompurin’s butt.

You could make an argument that, following back-to-back wins in the Sanrio Character Ranking election, Pompompurin has become as much the face of Sanrio as Hello Kitty is. You could make an even stronger argument, though, that Pompompurin is the butt of Sanrio, since depictions of the roly-poly golden retriever make consistently sure to include a prominent display of his butthole, or “the mark of his bottom,” as it’s euphemistically described. Many Japanese artists also make a point of depicting the buttholes of shiba inu in illustration, but in Pompompurin’s case it’s considered a critical part of his character design, with fans going so far as to consider it his “charm point,” so it’s got to be there, even sometimes when it means defying physics.

So when the time came to create the plush cushion that’s being included as an extra with the upcoming Pompompurin 30th Anniversary Nonbiri Pompom Book, the designers made the mark of his bottom the top priority. On the contoured side of the cushion, you can see Pompompurin’s hind feet and tail, but most importantly, the asterisk-shaped orifice. Flip the cushion around, and you’ll see Pompompurin with pals Muffin, Scone, and Bagel, but the fact that they’re just flat illustrations drives home how the backside is meant to be considered the primary side of this cushion.

You might have noticed that there are openings on either side of the cushion, and they allow you to pass your arms all the way through. Not only does this let you squeeze the cushion reassuringly tightly, it also means you can set it down on a desk or table and use it as a nap pillow. Yes, this will mean burying your face into Pompompurin’s butt, and the designers are well aware of that, including the invitation “Won’t you rest for a while with this cute butt?”

Further demonstrating the power of Pompompurin’s posterior, pre-orders for the Pompompurin 30th Anniversary Nonbiri Pompom Book with Soft and Squeezy Butt Cushion have already opened despite there being no solid information on what the book itself will contain. Then again, with the entire book being only 16 pages long, it’s not likely to be anything more than a few photo spreads and maybe a special thank-you message or two to fans, so really, this was always all about the butt.

The Pompompurin 30th Anniversary Nonbiri Pompom Book with Soft and Squeezy Butt Cushion is priced at 4,180 yen (US$26) and can be ordered through Amazon Japan here and Rakuten here, with shipping slated for September 9.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new coffee drinks… for people who don’t drink coffee
description: Created with Shibuya109 Lab, this new release aims to bridge the gap between traditional coffee and sweet Frappuccinos. This year marks the 30th anniversary for Starbucks in Japan, and the chain is celebrating the milestone with a number of new and innovative creations. Its latest release is particularly special, as the chain worked with Shibuya109 […]
content:
Created with Shibuya109 Lab, this new release aims to bridge the gap between traditional coffee and sweet Frappuccinos.

This year marks the 30th anniversary for Starbucks in Japan, and the chain is celebrating the milestone with a number of new and innovative creations. Its latest release is particularly special, as the chain worked with Shibuya109 lab, a youth marketing organisation based in Tokyo’s Shibuya district, to help create it.

The collaboration sought to understand how younger generations view coffee. It found that 46 percent of those surveyed had never tried black coffee, with many saying they thought it seemed bitter, while around 56 percent said they would drink coffee if it was sweet. Starbucks then got to work creating a new range of drinks to cater to those tastes.

Through workshops and tasting sessions, Starbucks discovered a gap between black coffee and sweet coffee drinks like lattes and Frappuccino beverages on the menu, and so fine-tuned the new beverages to enhance their drinkability and visual appeal.

The result is two new drinks that don’t fit the mold of traditional black coffee but aren’t as sweet as a Starbucks latte or Frappuccino.

▼ Clear Coffee (481 yen [US$3.26] for takeout; 490 yen dine-in) on the right, and Citrus Clear Coffee (579 yen takeout; 590 yen dine-in) on the left

The standard Clear Coffee is said to deliver a “gentle” coffee flavour with reduced bitterness and a subtle sweetness. Despite the lighter flavour profile, the aroma of coffee is still retained, providing a more approachable “first step” into the world of coffee for younger generations.

The Citrus Clear Coffee combines coffee with pieces of citrus fruit, creating a bright, refreshing flavour that helps to make coffee feel more familiar and approachable, especially during the hot summer months. The combination of fruit and coffee may sound unusual, but the company says the layered appearance of the drink, along with the ability to customise it with fruit pieces and syrup, is part of the experience.

▼ Both drinks use “Sumatra Masa Depan” coffee beans, which were developed to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the chain’s arrival in Japan.

Since opening its first Japanese store in Ginza in 1996, Starbucks has continued to develop new and exciting products for the local market, and these Clear Coffee drinks are a clever way to open the door to a new generation of drinkers. In fact, anyone who prefers a lighter coffee will likely be drawn to these drinks, and you can try them when they’re released on 31 July at Starbucks stores across Japan.

description: Two brews, inspired by the world of Final Fantasy XIV, are joining the taps at an Akihabara craft beer bar. content:
Two brews, inspired by the world of Final Fantasy XIV, are joining the taps at an Akihabara craft beer bar.

Back in the spring, Final Fantasy VII’s Seventh Heaven bar popped up in real-world Tokyo, letting fans stop by Tifa’s tavern for lemony cocktails personally endorsed by Soldier First Class Sephiroth. Sadly, Tokyo’s Seventh Heaven is now closed, but luckily there’s another spot in the city that’s going to be serving up some brand-new Final Fantasy-themed liquid refreshment.

Later this month, Exbar Tokyo Plus Akihabara, a craft beer bar in downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood, will be adding two Final Fantasy-themed beers to its taps, both of them nods to the world of Final Fantasy XIV. Inspired by the game’s Mothercrystal, Guiding Light is a fruit ale with a color as strikingly azure as the benevolent matronly mineral.

No less eye-catching in color is the brew evocative of Final Fantasy XIV’s vastly verdant city-state of Gridania, the Forest Healer. Exbar Tokyo Plus Akihabara says the Forest Healer is a “white ale,” though in this case they’re using the term in its sense of referring to a top-fermented wheat beer, since visually the Forest Healer is a vibrant green.

Though not run by Final Fantasy publisher Square Enix, Exbar Tokyo Plus Akihabara actually occupies the spot where the Square Enix Cafe (which is now located across town in the Shinjuku neighborhood) used to be. In addition to food and drinks, Exbar Tokyo Plus Akihabara also has an attached space for game-related merch, with its current tenant being the Final Fantasy XIV Goods Shop Akihabara. Coinciding with the start of the Final Fantasy XIV beers, the shop will be displaying a massive 160-centimeter (63-inch) tall illuminated Aetheryte crystal, and also offering key chains of adventurous Chocobo Alpha enjoying a round of cold ones with a Moogle buddy.

The Final Fantasy XIV beers will be served from July 31, the same day as the start of the Aetheryte display and key holder sales.
